chunks: He has forbidden carrion and blood and the flesh of the swine, and what has been killed in the name of any other but God; but if one is driven by necessity (to eat it) without craving or reverting to it, then God is forgiving and kind.

key_terms.الْمَيْتَة: Carrion (meat of an animal that died naturally)
key_terms.مَا أُهِلَّ لِغَيْرِ اللَّهِ بِهِ: What was sacrificed in the name of other than God

ai.seo_question: What are the four main forbidden foods in Islam and when is it permissible to eat them?
ai.summary: In Shia jurisprudence, this verse establishes the foundational categories of *najis* (impure) foods while introducing the principle of *darura* (necessity), which permits consumption only when survival is at stake and one is not acting with greed or habitual excess. The phrase 'what is sacrificed to other than Allah' is interpreted by scholars to include meat from non-Muslims who do not follow the Book, reinforcing the link between ritual purity and theological intent. This ruling is central to the distinction between mere dietary restriction and the spiritual discipline of avoiding *shirk* in daily sustenance.
